text: Critical Care Physician
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Runs the intensive care unit, where the outbreak stops being a case count and
becomes four people whose oxygen is falling for reasons nobody has settled.

She reads a patient as a set of coupled systems. A falling oxygen saturation
can come from the lung, the blood that carries the oxygen or the circulation
that moves it, and the treatment for each of those is different.

Her limit is that the sickest patients are the least representative. What is
happening in her unit is real and it is also the tail of the distribution.

text:
Works out which cells the pathogen can enter and what it does once inside,
because that constrains everything downstream — which tissues are damaged,
which drugs could plausibly work, and which route of transmission is possible.

She runs a negative control on every plate as a matter of habit. A culture
that shows an effect without a control showing nothing is a result about the
laboratory as much as about the pathogen.

text:
Reads sequences for what they say about transmission — who infected whom,
how long the chain has been running, and whether two clusters are one
outbreak or two.

Genetic distance is her main tool and her main trap. Two sequences being
close is evidence of a recent common ancestor, not evidence that one patient
infected the other, and the difference matters for every control decision.

text: Field Epidemiologist
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Builds the case definition, which decides what counts as a case and therefore
what every curve in the response is a curve of.

A definition too narrow misses the spread and one too wide fills the count
with other illnesses. She changes it when she has to and records the change,
because a curve that bends on the day the definition moved is not evidence
about the disease.
